Prior-odds adjustment for the probability of direction

Source: R/pd.adjust.R
pd.adjust.Rd

Decides which directional claims to make in a family of tests, from the probability of direction (pd) of each parameter. Two separate choices enter the decision. The threshold \(c\) (threshold) is the posterior probability required to make a claim. The bound \(\bar{\pi}\) (pi.max) is the largest prior probability allowed for either direction of a parameter, and sets how skeptical the prior may be about a claim. For each test the function returns pd and pd.adj, the posterior probability of the favored direction when that direction has prior probability \(1 - \bar{\pi}\). A direction is claimed when pd.adj is at least \(c\).

Usage

pd.adjust(
  pd = NULL,
  draws = NULL,
  p0 = NULL,
  pi.max = NULL,
  null.value = 0,
  direction = NULL,
  order = FALSE,
  threshold = 0.975,
  alpha = NULL
)

Arguments

pd

Numeric vector of pd values in \([0.5, 1]\). Every test is then treated as "two.sided" and direction is ignored. Ignored if draws is supplied.

draws

Matrix or data frame of posterior draws, one column per parameter. pd is computed from the draws according to direction and null.value.

p0

Number in \((0, 1)\). The largest prior probability that no claim in the family is correct, \(\Pr(H_0)\), from which \(\bar{\pi} = \Pr(H_0)^{1/m}\). Supply either p0 or pi.max, not both.

pi.max

Number in \((0, 1)\). The largest prior probability allowed for either direction of a parameter, chosen before the data. See Details for how to choose it. Values below 0.5 are set to 0.5, with a warning, so that no adjustment is made. Supply either pi.max or p0, not both.

null.value

Number or vector, the null value of each parameter on the scale of the draws. A single number applies to all parameters. Ignored when pd is supplied. Defaults to 0.

direction

Character vector with elements "two.sided", "greater", or "less", one per parameter, or a single value for all. NULL (the default) means "two.sided" for all.

order

Logical. If TRUE, rows are sorted by decreasing pd. If FALSE (the default), rows keep the order of the input.

threshold

Number in \((0.5, 1)\). The threshold \(c\), the posterior probability required to make a claim. Defaults to 0.975.

alpha

Optional number in \((0, 1)\). If supplied, the threshold is set to \(c = 1 - \alpha/2\) and threshold is ignored.

Value

An object of class pd_adjust, a data frame with one row per test and the columns pd, pd.adj, pi.max, m (the number of tests), and direction. With draws, it also has median.est (the posterior median) and null.value.

The thresholds are stored as attributes, threshold (\(c\)) and threshold.adj (\(c^*\)), together with alpha.nominal (\(2(1-c)\)) and alpha.eff (\(2(1-c^*)\)). The last two are per-test error rates only if pd is uniform on \([0.5, 1]\) for a null effect, which holds approximately under diffuse priors.

See print.pd_adjust and plot.pd_adjust.

Details

What is computed. pd comes from the fitted model, whose prior (the estimation prior) must be continuous and symmetric about null.value. Flat priors and symmetric priors centred on null.value, such as normal or Student-t priors, qualify. Each direction then has prior probability 0.5, and \(pd/(1 - pd)\) is the Bayes factor of the favored direction against the other.

With several tests, the prior odds of each claim are lowered (Jeffreys, 1938; Westfall et al., 1997). The direction of a claim is not known before the data, so the function considers every prior obtained by reweighting the two sides of the estimation prior so that each direction has prior probability between \(1 - \bar{\pi}\) and \(\bar{\pi}\). A claim must hold under all of these priors, and it is enough to check the one most skeptical of the favored direction, under which $$pd_{adj} = \frac{pd\,(1-\bar{\pi})}{pd\,(1-\bar{\pi}) + (1-pd)\,\bar{\pi}}.$$ The model is not refitted, and the posterior used for estimation is not changed.

The threshold on pd. The threshold \(c\) is not changed by the adjustment. Because \(pd_{adj}\) increases with pd, \(pd_{adj} \ge c\) holds exactly when pd reaches $$c^* = \frac{c\,\bar{\pi}}{(1-c)(1-\bar{\pi}) + c\,\bar{\pi}},$$ the value of pd required by \(c\) and \(\bar{\pi}\) together. The adjustment is thus equivalent to raising the threshold on pd from \(c\) to \(c^*\), reported as threshold.adj.

Choosing pi.max. pi.max says how skeptical you are of a directional claim before the data. With pi.max = 0.5 no adjustment is made. With pi.max = 0.8, a claim needs a Bayes factor four times larger. The same pi.max is used for every test, so the parameters should be exchangeable in direction, that is, no parameter is judged more likely than another to be positive or negative. They can be on different scales, because the sign of a parameter does not depend on its unit. The proportion of effects in the family that could be null is a reference value. If up to 70\ direction, so each direction should be allowed a prior probability as low as 0.3, which gives pi.max = 0.7. A larger value gives fewer false claims at a cost in power. The priors considered are continuous, so a null effect has probability zero under all of them, and pd.adj is the posterior probability of a sign. To test whether an effect is exactly null, use a prior that puts probability on the null value, such as a spike-and-slab prior. A narrower prior in the fitted model is no substitute, because a symmetric prior gives each direction prior probability 0.5 however narrow it is. Alternatively, p0 gives the largest prior probability that no claim in the family is correct. For parameters independent a priori, \(\bar{\pi} = \Pr(H_0)^{1/m}\), which grows with the number of tests \(m\).

Direction. With "two.sided", pd is the larger of \(\Pr(\theta > \theta_\text{null} \mid y)\) and \(\Pr(\theta < \theta_\text{null} \mid y)\), between 0.5 and 1. With "greater" or "less", pd is the posterior probability of the predicted side, between 0 and 1, and pd.adj is computed under the prior most skeptical of that side. The mode can differ from one test to another.

References

Berger, J. O. (1994). An overview of robust Bayesian analysis. Test, 3(1), 5–124. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02562676

Westfall, P. H., Johnson, W. O., & Utts, J. M. (1997). A Bayesian perspective on the Bonferroni adjustment. Biometrika, 84(2), 419–427. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/84.2.419

Jeffreys, H. (1938). Significance tests when several degrees of freedom arise simultaneously. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A. Mathematical and Physical Sciences, 165(921), 161–198. https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1938.0052

Storey, J. D. (2003). The positive false discovery rate: A Bayesian interpretation and the q-value. The Annals of Statistics, 31(6), 2013–2035. https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1074290335

Scott, J. G., & Berger, J. O. (2006). An exploration of aspects of Bayesian multiple testing. Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference, 136(7), 2144–2162. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jspi.2005.08.031

Scott, J. G., & Berger, J. O. (2010). Bayes and empirical-Bayes multiplicity adjustment in the variable- selection problem. The Annals of Statistics, 38(5), 2587–2619. https://doi.org/10.1214/10-AOS792

Examples

# From a vector of pd values
pd_values <- c(H1 = 0.999, H2 = 0.946, H3 = 0.813, H4 = 0.763,
H5 = 0.891, H6 = 0.987)
pd.adjust(pd = pd_values, p0 = 0.4)
#> Prior-odds adjustment for directional claims
#>   m = 6, pi.max = 0.8584
#>   c = 0.975, c* = 0.9958
#>   direction = two.sided
#> 
#>       pd pd.adj
#> H1 0.999 0.9940
#> H2 0.946 0.7430
#> H3 0.813 0.4177
#> H4 0.763 0.3469
#> H5 0.891 0.5742
#> H6 0.987 0.9261
#> 
#> pd.adj: pd when the favored direction has prior probability 1 - pi.max.

# The same, giving pi.max directly
pd.adjust(pd = pd_values, pi.max = 0.4^(1/6))
#> Prior-odds adjustment for directional claims
#>   m = 6, pi.max = 0.8584
#>   c = 0.975, c* = 0.9958
#>   direction = two.sided
#> 
#>       pd pd.adj
#> H1 0.999 0.9940
#> H2 0.946 0.7430
#> H3 0.813 0.4177
#> H4 0.763 0.3469
#> H5 0.891 0.5742
#> H6 0.987 0.9261
#> 
#> pd.adj: pd when the favored direction has prior probability 1 - pi.max.

# Simulate draws
Sigma <- matrix(0, nrow = 6, ncol = 6); diag(Sigma) <- 1
mu    <- c(1, -0.1, 0.8, 0, 2, 3)
draws <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = 4000, mu = mu, Sigma = Sigma)
colnames(draws) <- c("H1", "H2", "H3", "H4", "H5", "H6")

# From posterior draws
pd.adjust(draws = draws, pi.max = 0.7, null.value = 0)
#> Prior-odds adjustment for directional claims
#>   m = 6, pi.max = 0.7
#>   c = 0.975, c* = 0.9891
#>   null value = 0, direction = two.sided
#> 
#>    median.est     pd pd.adj
#> H1     0.9860 0.8358 0.6856
#> H2    -0.1175 0.5350 0.3302
#> H3     0.7761 0.7822 0.6062
#> H4    -0.0089 0.5030 0.3025
#> H5     1.9500 0.9762 0.9463
#> H6     2.9866 0.9995 0.9988
#> 
#> pd.adj: pd when the favored direction has prior probability 1 - pi.max.

# Rows sorted by decreasing pd
pd.adjust(draws = draws, pi.max = 0.7, null.value = 0, order = TRUE)
#> Prior-odds adjustment for directional claims
#>   m = 6, pi.max = 0.7
#>   c = 0.975, c* = 0.9891
#>   null value = 0, direction = two.sided
#> 
#>    median.est     pd pd.adj
#> H6     2.9866 0.9995 0.9988
#> H5     1.9500 0.9762 0.9463
#> H1     0.9860 0.8358 0.6856
#> H3     0.7761 0.7822 0.6062
#> H2    -0.1175 0.5350 0.3302
#> H4    -0.0089 0.5030 0.3025
#> 
#> pd.adj: pd when the favored direction has prior probability 1 - pi.max.

# Different directions and null values across parameters
pd.adjust(draws = draws, pi.max = 0.6, null.value = c(0.2, 0, 0.2, 0, 0.5, 0.5),
          direction = c("greater", "two.sided", "greater",
          "two.sided", "greater", "greater"))
#> Prior-odds adjustment for directional claims
#>   m = 6, pi.max = 0.6
#>   c = 0.975, c* = 0.9832
#> 
#>    median.est null.value     pd pd.adj direction
#> H1     0.9860        0.2 0.7820 0.7051   greater
#> H2    -0.1175        0.0 0.5350 0.4341 two.sided
#> H3     0.7761        0.2 0.7230 0.6350   greater
#> H4    -0.0089        0.0 0.5030 0.4029 two.sided
#> H5     1.9500        0.5 0.9285 0.8965   greater
#> H6     2.9866        0.5 0.9948 0.9921   greater
#> 
#> pd.adj: pd when the favored direction has prior probability 1 - pi.max.
